items.stem: Which of the following best describes "public-health campaign"?
options: A design feature that steers people towards a choice without forcing it
An instruction that tells the audience what to do
A campaign whose message is adapted for posters, social media, video and other platforms
A coordinated set of texts designed to change health-related behaviour in a population
items.answer: A coordinated set of texts designed to change health-related behaviour in a population
items.markingKey: D. "public-health campaign" is a coordinated set of texts designed to change health-related behaviour in a population.

items.stem: Explain why public-health campaigns combine emotional appeals with practical help.
items.answer: Emotion motivates, but without a clear, achievable action (a helpline) motivation may produce anxiety rather than change.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Emotion motivates, but without a clear, achievable action (a helpline) motivation may produce anxiety rather than change. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a public-health campaign and a commercial advertisement.
items.answer: A commercial advertisement aims to sell a product for profit; a public-health campaign aims to change behaviour for social benefit, though both use persuasive techniques.
items.markingKey: A commercial advertisement aims to sell a product for profit; a public-health campaign aims to change behaviour for social benefit, though both use persuasive techniques. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following home-front poster from a fictional wartime nation, written in the style of 1940s propaganda.

[Image: a woman in overalls rolls up her sleeve beside a factory gate; behind her, the silhouettes of marching soldiers.]
THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT.
YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE.
Every shell you make is a letter home.
Don't let them down – report for factory work today.

Identify the intended audience of this propaganda poster. Support your answer with one reference to the text.
items.answer: Women at home during wartime who could be recruited for industrial work.
items.markingKey: Women at home during wartime who could be recruited for industrial work. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following direct-mail appeal letter from an international charity.

Dear Friend,
This is Amina. She is seven. Every morning she walks two hours to collect water that makes her sick.
[Photograph: a thin girl with downcast eyes holds a yellow jerrycan.]
For just 5 euros a month, you can change Amina's life forever.
Please don't turn the page.

State the main purpose of the text and explain how one feature helps to achieve it.
items.answer: To prompt an immediate monthly donation through pity and guilt. Supporting feature: "Please don't turn the page." (emotive imperative) – it makes turning the page feel like abandoning her.
items.markingKey: To prompt an immediate monthly donation through pity and guilt. Supporting feature: "Please don't turn the page." (emotive imperative) – it makes turning the page feel like abandoning her. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Design a cross-platform campaign (poster, social post and short video concept) to encourage teenagers to sleep more, and justify how each text suits its platform.
items.answer: Indicative content: consistent message; platform-specific conventions; appeals; call to action.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: consistent message; platform-specific conventions; appeals; call to action.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A campaign whose message is adapted for posters, social media, video and other platforms"?
options: informed consent
white saviour narrative
fear appeal
cross-platform campaign
items.answer: cross-platform campaign
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of cross-platform campaign.

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Public-health campaigns simply inform people of facts." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They are persuasive texts that use emotional appeals, imagery and calls to action, not just information.

items.stem:
Read the following poster from a refugee-aid NGO campaign.

[Image: a child's crayon drawing of a house with a red roof and a yellow sun, pinned to the canvas wall of a tent. No people are shown.]
'Home is a place she has only drawn.'
'For three years, Leila has lived in a camp. With your help, her drawing can become an address.'
Text HOME to donate.

Discuss the relationship between image and words in this text.
items.answer: The bright drawing against the drab tent canvas contrasts hope and reality; the absence of faces avoids exploitation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "white saviour narrative"?
options: A design feature that steers people towards a choice without forcing it
A representation in which (usually Western) donors or outsiders rescue passive victims
Imagery that exploits the suffering of poor people to provoke pity and donations, often reinforcing stereotypes
An instruction that tells the audience what to do
items.answer: A representation in which (usually Western) donors or outsiders rescue passive victims
items.markingKey: B. "white saviour narrative" is a representation in which (usually Western) donors or outsiders rescue passive victims.

items.stem: Briefly explain why some NGOs now avoid images of suffering.
items.answer: They seek to respect dignity, obtain consent, avoid compassion fatigue and represent beneficiaries as active people.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They seek to respect dignity, obtain consent, avoid compassion fatigue and represent beneficiaries as active people. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following direct-mail appeal letter from an international charity.

Dear Friend,
This is Amina. She is seven. Every morning she walks two hours to collect water that makes her sick.
[Photograph: a thin girl with downcast eyes holds a yellow jerrycan.]
For just 5 euros a month, you can change Amina's life forever.
Please don't turn the page.

Evaluate the ethics of the representation in this text.
items.answer: The appeal individualises suffering effectively but represents Amina as helpless and the donor as saviour; the promise of changing her life "forever" for 5 euros oversimplifies poverty and denies her agency.

items.stem:
Read the following photograph and caption from a contemporary documentary series on fast fashion, described in words.

[A young woman sits at a sewing machine in a long row of identical machines under flickering fluorescent light. In the blurred foreground lies a heap of bright T-shirts with price tags reading '4.99'.]
Caption: 'Shift 2 of 2. Rina, 19, sews 120 collars an hour.'

Guiding question: How does the photograph make the viewer reconsider cheap clothing?
Write an analytical paragraph that answers the guiding question.
items.answer: Thesis: the image connects the price tag to the person. (1) Foreground/background composition. (2) Repetition of machines. (3) Naming caption with statistic. Evaluation: naming Rina restores individuality, unlike older documentary practice.
items.markingKey: Thesis: the image connects the price tag to the person. (1) Foreground/background composition. (2) Repetition of machines. (3) Naming caption with statistic. Evaluation: naming Rina restores individuality, unlike older documentary practice. Markbands (criteria A–D). The use of "we" to speak on behalf of a group
A public declaration of the beliefs, aims and demands of a group or movement

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a youth climate movement's manifesto.

WE ARE NOT ASKING.
1. We demand that our city ends approval of new fossil-fuel projects by 2030.
2. We demand climate education in every school, in every subject.
3. We demand a seat at every table where our future is decided.
We are told to be patient. Patience is a luxury for those who will not live with the consequences. Join us.

Identify the device used in "We demand ... We demand ... We demand" and explain its effect.
items.answer: Anaphora: "We demand ... We demand ... We demand" – repetition builds collective force and clarity.
items.markingKey: Anaphora: "We demand ... We demand ... We demand" – repetition builds collective force and clarity. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student delegate at an international youth climate summit.

Delegates, I was born in 2008. In my lifetime the sea outside my grandmother's house in Tuvalu has crept forty metres closer. Forty metres. You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps. You tell us we are the future. But we are not the future – we are the present, standing in water. So do not applaud me. Applause is cheap. Act.

Explain how the context of the text shapes its meaning or its reception.
items.answer: Delivered at a summit where young speakers are often celebrated but not listened to; Tuvalu is a low-lying Pacific nation highly vulnerable to sea-level rise, which gives the personal anecdote political force.
items.markingKey: Delivered at a summit where young speakers are often celebrated but not listened to; Tuvalu is a low-lying Pacific nation highly vulnerable to sea-level rise, which gives the personal anecdote political force. items.stem:
Read the following speech by a city mayor at the opening of a public library in a multilingual neighbourhood.

Friends, neighbours – bienvenidos, karibu, welcome. Some people say libraries are relics, that everything we need is on our phones. But a phone cannot hold a child's hand through her first chapter book. A phone does not stay open late for the night-shift nurse who wants to finish her degree. This building belongs to you: to every language spoken on these streets, and to every language not yet learned.

Comment on the writer's choice of language in "A phone cannot ... A phone does not".
items.answer: Anaphora: "A phone cannot ... A phone does not" – repeating the subject at the start of successive sentences hammers home what technology cannot do.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a campaigner for women's suffrage at a public meeting in Manchester, 1912 (an original pastiche written for study).

Gentlemen of the press, you call us unreasonable. Very well. Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes on a shop she ran for thirty years, yet could not vote for the men who spent them? Was it reasonable that the law counted her as a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing? We have asked politely for forty years. Politeness has been answered with silence. We shall not be silent any longer.

Explain the effect of the personification "Politeness has been answered with silence" on the reader.
items.answer: Personification: "Politeness has been answered with silence" – making politeness and silence actors summarises decades of ignored petitions in one image.
items.markingKey: Personification: "Politeness has been answered with silence" – making politeness and silence actors summarises decades of ignored petitions in one image. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following public-health campaign poster against smoking.

[Image: a close-up of a toddler's hand reaching for a cigarette packet on a coffee table.]
Headline: 'They copy everything you do.'
Below: 'Children who grow up with smokers are much more likely to start smoking themselves.'
Call to action: 'Quit for them. Free support: QuitLine.'

What ethical questions does this campaign text raise?
items.answer: The poster uses a child to provoke guilt; it avoids graphic images but could stigmatise parents who smoke; offering free support balances the guilt with help.
items.markingKey: The poster uses a child to provoke guilt; it avoids graphic images but could stigmatise parents who smoke; offering free support balances the guilt with help. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following direct-mail appeal letter from an international charity.

Dear Friend,
This is Amina. She is seven. Every morning she walks two hours to collect water that makes her sick.
[Photograph: a thin girl with downcast eyes holds a yellow jerrycan.]
For just 5 euros a month, you can change Amina's life forever.
Please don't turn the page.

Explain how the writer signals who the intended audience is.
items.answer: Potential donors in wealthy countries receiving the letter at home.
items.markingKey: Potential donors in wealthy countries receiving the letter at home. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a disability-rights activist at a rally outside a parliament.

They say we ask for special treatment. Ramps are not special. Captions are not special. A lift that works is not special. What is special is a parliament with three hundred steps and not one ramp to its public gallery. We have watched our laws being made from the pavement for long enough. Nothing about us, without us.

How does the move from listing to the image of watching laws "from the pavement" shape the reader's experience of the text?
items.answer: The move from listing to the image of watching laws "from the pavement": the concrete image makes exclusion visible and physical.
items.markingKey: The move from listing to the image of watching laws "from the pavement": the concrete image makes exclusion visible and physical. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

Read the following public-health campaign poster against smoking.

Headline: 'They copy everything you do.'
Below: 'Children who grow up with smokers are much more likely to start smoking themselves.'
Call to action: 'Quit for them. Free support: QuitLine.'

Guiding question: How does the poster use the image of a child to persuade its audience?
Write an analytical paragraph that answers the guiding question.
items.answer: Thesis: the poster turns parental love into motivation. (1) Close-up of the hand. (2) Direct address and the verb "copy". (3) The imperative and offer of support. Evaluation: guilt can motivate but may alienate.

items.stem: A student claims: "Public-health campaigns simply inform people of facts." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They are persuasive texts that use emotional appeals, imagery and calls to action, not just information.
items.markingKey: They are persuasive texts that use emotional appeals, imagery and calls to action, not just information. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student delegate at an international youth climate summit.

Delegates, I was born in 2008. In my lifetime the sea outside my grandmother's house in Tuvalu has crept forty metres closer. Forty metres. You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps. You tell us we are the future. But we are not the future – we are the present, standing in water. So do not applaud me. Applause is cheap. Act.

How might knowledge of the context of production help a reader to interpret this speech?
items.answer: Delivered at a summit where young speakers are often celebrated but not listened to; Tuvalu is a low-lying Pacific nation highly vulnerable to sea-level rise, which gives the personal anecdote political force.
items.markingKey: Delivered at a summit where young speakers are often celebrated but not listened to; Tuvalu is a low-lying Pacific nation highly vulnerable to sea-level rise, which gives the personal anecdote political force. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Charities are justified in using shocking images if they save lives."
items.answer: Shock may be effective, but ethical campaigns seek ways to motivate without exploitation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: funds raised have real benefits; shock overcomes indifference. Arguments against: it reinforces stereotypes; it can violate dignity and consent. Supported judgement: Shock may be effective, but ethical campaigns seek ways to motivate without exploitation.

items.stem:
Read the following poster from a refugee-aid NGO campaign.

[Image: a child's crayon drawing of a house with a red roof and a yellow sun, pinned to the canvas wall of a tent. No people are shown.]
'Home is a place she has only drawn.'
'For three years, Leila has lived in a camp. With your help, her drawing can become an address.'
Text HOME to donate.

Guiding question: How does the poster represent the refugee child, and with what ethical effects?
Write one analytical paragraph that answers the guiding question, using at least two references to the text.
items.answer: Thesis: the poster seeks empathy without exploitation. (1) The drawing as metonymy. (2) Absence of faces. (3) The shift from drawing to address. Evaluation: more dignified than many appeals, though it still centres the donor.

items.stem: "An uncompromising tone makes a manifesto more effective." Discuss.
items.answer: It energises the base but may limit wider persuasion.
